Moral Foundations Theory is a framework that separates human morality into the following categories:

  - Care/Harm: related to our long evolution as mammals with attachment systems
    and an ability to feel (and dislike) the pain of others. It underlies the
    virtues of kindness, gentleness, and nurturance.

  - Loyalty/Betrayal: related to our long history as tribal creatures able to
    form shifting coalitions. It is active anytime people feel that it is "one
    for all and all for one." It underlies the virtues of patriotism and
    self-sacrifice for the group.

  - Authority/Subversion: shaped by our long primate history of hierarchical
    social interactions. It underlies virtues of leadership and followership,
    including deference to prestigious authority figures and respect for
    traditions.

  - Sanctity/Purity: shaped by the psychology of disgust and contamination. It
    underlies notions of striving to live in an elevated, less carnal, more
    noble, and more "natural" way (often present in religious narratives). This
    foundation underlies the widespread idea that the body is a temple that can
    be desecrated by immoral activities and contaminants (an idea not unique to
    religious traditions). It underlies the virtues of self-discipline,
    self-improvement, naturalness, and spirituality.

  - Equality: related to our intuitions about equal treatment and equal outcome
    for individuals.

  - Proportionality: related to our intuitions about individuals getting
    rewarded in proportion to their merit or contribution.

# UK Independence Party (UKIP) Manifesto 2010 Summary

## Core Mission: Withdrawal from the European Union

The UKIP 2010 manifesto centres on the fundamental belief that Britain must leave the EU to regain three essential freedoms: freedom of action (self-governance without Brussels interference), freedom of resources (reclaiming the estimated £6.4 billion net annual contribution), and freedom of the people (democratic control over British affairs).

## Economic Policy

UKIP proposes dramatic tax simplification, including a flat tax of 31% with a raised personal allowance of £11,500 to remove minimum wage earners from taxation. The party advocates abolishing Employers' National Insurance over five years, eliminating Inheritance Tax, and scrapping over 120,000 EU regulations burdening British businesses. They propose replacing VAT with a Local Sales Tax and reducing public sector employment to 1997 levels.

The manifesto outlines ambitious investment programmes totalling billions annually in defence equipment, nuclear power stations, flood defences, transport infrastructure, and prison building—designed to create approximately one million new skilled manufacturing jobs.

## Immigration and Border Control

UKIP demands an immediate five-year freeze on immigration for permanent settlement, with future immigration capped at 50,000 annually. They propose tripling UK Borders Agency staff to 30,000, ending amnesty for illegal immigrants, repealing the Human Rights Act, and withdrawing from the European Convention on Human Rights. The party explicitly opposes multiculturalism, favouring "uniculturalism" to create a single British identity.

## Public Services

**Healthcare:** While maintaining NHS principles of free care, UKIP proposes elected County Health Boards, abolishing Strategic Health Authorities and Primary Care Trusts, and franchising NHS services to private and charitable organisations.

**Education:** The manifesto advocates School Vouchers allowing parental choice, retention and expansion of grammar schools, scrapping the 50% university target, and replacing student loans with grants. Elected County Education Boards would replace Local Education Authorities.

**Pensions:** UKIP proposes a simplified, non-means tested Citizen's Pension of £130 weekly for all over-65s, while bringing public sector pensions "back into line" with private provision.

## Defence and Security

The party pledges a 40% increase in defence spending, expanding the Army by 25%, restoring the Royal Navy, and maintaining the independent nuclear deterrent. On law and order, UKIP advocates doubling prison capacity, introducing "three strikes" sentencing, scrapping the Human Rights Act, and withdrawing from the European Arrest Warrant.

## Energy and Environment

UKIP takes a sceptical stance on man-made climate change, proposing to repeal the Climate Change Act, halt renewable energy subsidies, and expand nuclear power to provide 50% of electricity needs. They advocate supporting coal extraction and opposing wind farms.

## Constitutional Reform

The manifesto proposes "Direct Democracy" through binding referenda, proportional representation via Alternative Vote Plus, elected local boards for police, education and health, and abolition of regional government. UKIP supports retaining the monarchy and opposes Church of England disestablishment.

## Cultural Identity

The party promotes "civic nationalism" and "Britishness," proposing to ban the burqa in public buildings, deport radical preachers, create St George's Day and Commonwealth Day public holidays, and safeguard British weights and measures from EU metrication.

## Agriculture and Fishing

UKIP promises withdrawal from the Common Agricultural Policy and Common Fisheries Policy, restoration of British fishing grounds with a 200-mile Exclusive Economic Zone, and support for British farmers through labelling campaigns and fair pricing rather than subsidies.

The manifesto presents a comprehensive Eurosceptic vision positioning EU withdrawal as the solution to Britain's economic, immigration, democratic, and cultural challenges—the foundation upon which all other policy proposals rest.

# Labour Party Manifesto 2010 Summary: A Future Fair for All

The 2010 Labour Party Manifesto presents a progressive vision for national renewal during challenging times, positioning itself against what it characterises as Conservative pessimism and privilege for the few.

## Economic Recovery and Reform
Labour commits to securing economic recovery through continued public spending support, rejecting "reckless cuts" that could push Britain back into recession. The manifesto pledges to halve the deficit by 2014 through economic growth, fair taxation (including the 50p top tax rate), and targeted spending cuts. Banking reform features prominently, with commitments to tighter regulation, greater capital requirements, and breaking up government-owned banks while protecting building societies. The manifesto emphasises building a diverse, high-tech economy through a £4 billion UK Finance for Growth fund, investment in green industries, High Speed Rail, and universal broadband access.

## Fairness and Social Justice
Central to Labour's vision is ensuring prosperity is shared fairly. Key commitments include maintaining the National Minimum Wage rising with earnings, a £40-per-week "Better Off in Work" guarantee, and abolishing long-term unemployment through job guarantees. First-time buyers receive stamp duty exemption on properties under £250,000, funded by higher rates on million-pound homes. A new People's Bank through the Post Office and clamping down on exploitative lending demonstrate commitment to financial fairness.

## Public Services
Labour pledges increased frontline spending on education, with free nursery places, one-to-one tuition guarantees, and 75% of young people reaching higher education or advanced apprenticeships. For the NHS, legally binding patient guarantees include 18-week maximum waiting times and one-week cancer test results, alongside preventative healthcare expansion. A new National Care Service promises free home care for those with greatest needs and protection of homes from care charges after two years.

## Community and Security
The manifesto commits to maintaining police numbers, neighbourhood teams, and faster action on anti-social behaviour. Immigration will be controlled through an Australian-style points-based system. Democratic renewal includes referenda on voting reform and House of Lords elections, fixed-term parliaments, and movement toward a Written Constitution.

## Progressive Values
Throughout, Labour positions itself as the party of active, reforming government against Conservative "absent government," arguing that fairness, opportunity, and collective responsibility—not market forces alone—create prosperity and security for all.
